Our rates include $\widetilde{O}(1/T)$ for convex Euclidean-Lipschitz optimization over the $\ell_1$-ball, improving on the $O(1/\sqrt{T})$ classical rate under general assumptions. The key technical device is a new online learning game, where the comparator is evaluated using the maximum of affine losses observed so far. We bound the value of this game above and below in terms of a combinatorial online learning quantity: the sequential fat-shattering dimension, which we characterize for the $\ell_p / \ell_q$ case. Our results generally apply when the feasible set $\mathcal{X}$ and the set of possible subgradients $\mathcal{H}$ admit a type of minimax theorem, advancing on a fundamental question by Sridharan (Sri12, Section 10.1.2, Q3). As a geometric consequence of our analysis, of independent interest, we obtain estimates for the expected distance of a convex hull of samples to their mean in several Banach geometries, a version of the celebrated Wendel's theorem (Wen62), but quantitative and for bounded general distributions as opposed to centrally symmetric ones.
comment: Polished writing. Small additions (quasar-convex optimization, clarification regarding optimizing in a subset...)

title: Stable Movement for Nondual Lipschitz Convex Optimization: Efficiency and Nearly Optimal Oracle Rates
comments: polished writing, added a few more general results (such as a better lower bound, and a more general potential-energy center)
summary: We study efficient algorithms for realizing the first-order oracle complexity of optimization of $G$-Lipschitz convex functions with respect to the $\ell_q$-norm over an $\ell_p$-ball of radius $R$, where $1\leq p,q\leq\infty$. For $p<q$, we obtain error $\widetilde{O}_{p,q}(GR/T^{1/p-(1/q-1/2)_{+}})$ after $T$ oracle queries, attaining the lower bounds in a COLT 2015 open problem (Guz15b) with efficient algorithms. In particular, the rate is $\widetilde{O}(GR/T)$ for Euclidean Lipschitzness with an $\ell_1$-ball domain of radius $R$ ($p=1,q=2$). Our solution consists of reducing convex Lipschitz optimization to the chasing nested convex sets problem (BBE+20) in sublevel sets of an evolving maximum of affine lower bounds, that is, the bundle (LNN95): at each query we either find a point with low function value or we produce a deep cut in the current sublevel of the bundle that we chase. The dichotomy between stability of selectors and forced movement by deep cuts bounds the number of iterations of the algorithm nearly optimally. For nested convex subsets of the $\ell_p$ ball $R B_p^d$, we introduce novel stable selectors whose movement is nearly optimal in high dimensions. A Monte Carlo average of the proposed selector achieves near-optimal rates with high probability and can be implemented for our optimization algorithm in polynomial time in the real-arithmetic model.
comment: polished writing, added a few more general results (such as a better lower bound, and a more general potential-energy center)

title: Forecasting Brain Tracer Distribution from Pre-Contrast MRI: A Comparison of Direct Regression and Flow Matching
summary: The brain fluid clearance system can be studied with intrathecal contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). By injecting a tracer into the spinal canal and performing MRI over 24--48\,h, one can measure how a tracer injected into the cerebrospinal fluid spreads through the brain. As this is an invasive procedure requiring several MRI scans, we ask how much of the later tracer distribution can be predicted from the pre-contrast scan and elapsed time alone. Using 104 training patients (878 MRI volumes), we compared a direct image-to-image regression model with a more complex generative model based on conditional flow matching, and tested both on 23 held-out patients and on 51 patients from a separate cohort with idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus (iNPH). Relative to simply copying the pre-contrast scan, the direct model reduced the mean absolute error (intensities normalized to $[0,1]$) from 0.089 to 0.036, about 60\%, in held-out patients and from 0.075 to 0.056, about 25\%, in the iNPH cohort. The reduction held in every sampled elapsed-time interval and brain compartment, and errors remained largest at 20--30\,h and in the ventricles, where enhancement is strongest. Its predicted change maps agreed with the observed tracer enhancement rather than only reproducing anatomy. The generative model was less accurate in both cohorts. A substantial part of the later tracer distribution is therefore predictable from the patient's brain anatomy as seen on pre-contrast MRI, and the added model complexity gave no benefit at this data scale. Whether this accuracy suffices for a given clinical use remains to be established; with prospective validation, such forecasts could help simplify the MRI protocol used to assess brain clearance.

title: When Pass@$k$ Crossovers Are Real - and Why: Paired Inference and the Markov Kernel of RLVR
comments: 47 pages, 8 figures. Revised title, expanded experiments and analysis, and updated author list
summary:
Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) typically improves pass@1 but can fall behind its base model at large sampling budgets $k$, commonly interpreted as sharpening existing solutions. Because adjacent pass@$k$ estimates reuse generations, pointwise error bars cannot establish a crossover. We formulate paired inference on the RL-minus-base difference curve: a prompt-level multiplier bootstrap yields a one-sided dominance test and simultaneous confidence bands requiring both an early gain and a later loss. Among nine public RLVR checkpoints at 3k-16k token limits, only one narrowly meets this criterion before multiplicity adjustment; asymmetric truncation can create, mask, or reverse crossovers. On 1,060 deduplicated competition problems at 32k tokens, two 1.5B models exhibit certified crossovers around $k\approx10$-$60$, while two 7B models show no supported loss. A paired variance decomposition shows why adding prompts improves power more than deeper sampling.
  Prompts with identical base success probability diverge after RLVR, with dispersion replicating across independent generation halves and violating Lipschitz slope bounds for reasonable deterministic maps. Modeling RLVR as a Markov kernel, Jensen's inequality shows that conditional dispersion depresses pass@$k$ for $k\ge2$. Once dispersion is modeled, the conditional-mean log-odds slope is below one in every pair: RLVR improves hard prompts on average, while late-$k$ loss comes from a 2%-3% minority of base-solved prompts collapsing onto a repeated modal wrong answer and resisting prefix rescue up to 4,096 tokens. In controlled runs from one base model on 3,000 new problems, all four GRPO arms fall behind near $k\approx200$ and remain behind through $k=4096$, while SFT stays significantly ahead throughout.
comment: 47 pages, 8 figures. Revised title, expanded experiments and analysis, and updated author list

title: Word Length and Diameter in Permutation Groups
summary: In the binary diameter problem, the input consists of explicitly given permutations generating a finite group $G$ and a binary-encoded number $k$, and the question is whether every element of $G$ is a product of at most $k$ of the given generators. In the binary length problem, the input additionally contains a permutation $g \in G$, and the question is whether $g$ is such a product. We show that the binary diameter problem is PSPACE-complete, thereby confirming a conjecture of Lohrey and Rosowski (2023). Moreover, we show that PSPACE-hardness already holds for solvable groups of derived length at most 3, whereas the problem is $Π_2^{\mathrm{P}}$-complete for 2-step nilpotent groups. For the binary length problem, we establish a sharp complexity threshold: the problem is NP-complete for 2-step nilpotent groups, which extends a result of Lohrey and Rosowski for abelian groups, and PSPACE-complete for groups that are simultaneously 3-step nilpotent and metabelian, which strengthens the main result of Jerrum (1985). Finally, we show that the unary diameter problem, where $k$ is encoded in unary, is $Π_2^{\mathrm{P}}$-complete for generating sets of the full symmetric group, confirming another conjecture of Lohrey and Rosowski.

title: Quantum Advantage for Distributed Symmetry Breaking
summary: We present a distributed quantum algorithm that $3$-colors cycles in $O(1)$ rounds, with high probability. It follows that all locally checkable labeling problems (LCLs) that have round complexity $O(\log^* n)$ in the classical LOCAL model can be solved in $O(1)$ rounds in the quantum-LOCAL model, with high probability; this includes problems such as maximal independent set and maximal matching in bounded-degree graphs. This presents the first natural examples of graph problems with an asymptotic distributed quantum advantage for the LOCAL model; all prior examples that separate LOCAL and quantum-LOCAL are artificial problems constructed merely for the sake of demonstrating quantum advantage.

title: Emergence in Network Systems is Bounded by Boundary-Crossing Paths
summary: Emergence, features of a whole that no part shows alone, is central to complex systems but rarely measured so as to locate its source. Viewing a system structurally, as a network of interacting parts, we evaluate emergence as what observing the coupled whole reveals beyond, or erases from, the combined observations of the parts. For observations that build what they see route by route, we show that every emergent feature is produced by its own route across the interface between parts, a route that traces it to the components and interactions responsible. We show the number of all such boundary-crossing paths bounds the total emergence discrepancy, and equals the emergence of measures that count routes. The bound is computed locally around the interface, validated through network examples, and in a nervous system the routes show that interneurons relay most of the emergence. Our work associates emergence with path structure in the network system that can be anticipated, attributed, and engineered.

title: A Tale of Two Walks: From Kac to KMP and Back
summary:
We reveal an unexpected connection between two interacting particle systems: Kac's walk and the Kipnis-Marchioro-Presutti (KMP) process. We first establish a mixing-time analogue of Aldous's conjecture for the KMP process on general graphs: the mixing time of the $t$-particle process on any connected $d$-vertex graph is at most $O(\log d)$ times the corresponding single-particle mixing time, uniformly in $t$. As an application, we improve the mixing-time bound for coordinate hit-and-run on the $n$-dimensional standard simplex from $\widetilde{O}(n^3)$ [KV26] to $O(n\log n)$, while removing the dependence on the initial distribution. We then show that the twirling channel induced by the parallel Kac's walk on the symmetric subspace can be exactly encoded by a Markov chain on partitions, which naturally lifts to a parallel KMP chain on the complete graph. We prove that $O(\log d+\log(1/\varepsilon))$ repetitions of the parallel Kac's walk suffice to approximate Haar twirling on the symmetric subspace of $(\mathbb{C}^d)^{\otimes t}$ to error $\varepsilon$, uniformly in all $t$.
  Our main technical contribution is a new structural property of KMP-type dynamics: conditional product structure, which holds for both the standard KMP processes on general graphs and the parallel KMP processes on complete graphs. Conditioned on suitable auxiliary randomness, the evolution of the labeled KMP process factorizes into independent single-particle updates. Combining this structure with an exact coupling, we remove the dependence on the number of particles from the mixing bounds for both unlabeled KMP models. This bypasses the $\log(π_{\min}^{-1})$ dependency from spectral-gap arguments, which is often prohibitively large for many-particle systems. Using this framework, we prove mixing bounds that are sharp up to logarithmic factors for both unlabeled KMP models.

title: Robust and leakage-resilient device-independent oblivious transfer in MiniQCrypt
comments: v3: Improved robustness and leakage tolerance, now allowing constant rates of noise and leakage
summary:
Assuming post-quantum one-way functions, we construct device-independent oblivious transfer and bit commitment that tolerate independent honest faults at a constant rate and adaptive, bidirectional quantum leakage between the laboratories at a constant rate. Honest parties use trusted classical computation to operate untrusted quantum devices, which may share arbitrary entanglement and perform joint measurements without assumptions of independence or identical distribution. Security is simulation-based against quantum polynomial-time adversaries and composes sequentially with efficient simulators. For security parameter $λ$ and a prescribed total leakage budget $\ell$, one complete one-bit oblivious transfer uses $Θ(\ell+\log^2λ)$ device coordinates in at most three single-use device windows, including preprocessing, and polynomial classical computation and communication. The leakage budget is shared across these windows. The commitment has efficient simulators against both parties and yields device-independent coin tossing with abort; each uses one window. Completeness of oblivious transfer gives device-independent secure computation with abort for every efficiently computable classical functionality on a fixed number of parties, against static corruption of any proper subset, provided each reached call to oblivious transfer satisfies the device and budget conditions.
  The construction combines short selectors with code-based choice masking, a global audit, and error correction across field symbols. The commitment extractor changes a classical code coset while leaving the device execution and its leakage unchanged. Sender security uses a global Fourier analysis and a selector-aware Magic Square repetition bound derived from the two-round threshold theorem of Kundu and Tan (2023).
comment: v3: Improved robustness and leakage tolerance, now allowing constant rates of noise and leakage

title: Counterexamples to the Strong Roberson Conjecture
comments: 24 pages. v2: expanded introduction, related work and conclusion; improved exposition throughout; smaller explicit counterexamples obtained
summary: We refute the Strong Roberson Conjecture, which asserts that adding any graph outside a graph class closed under minors and disjoint unions strictly increases the distinguishing power of homomorphism counts from that class. More precisely, we construct connected graphs $H$ for which homomorphism counts from graphs excluding $H$ as a minor determine the number of homomorphisms from $H$ to any target graph. We also refute the analogous conjecture with immersions in place of minors. The proof introduces a method for deriving exact homomorphism count dependence from modular equivalences. We obtain these modular equivalences for infinitely many primes using prime-order automorphisms and the corresponding orbit quotients. We complete the refutations by proving that suitable circulant graphs with two jump lengths and related cubic bipartite graphs exclude their corresponding orbit quotients as minors and immersions, respectively.
comment: 24 pages. v2: expanded introduction, related work and conclusion; improved exposition throughout; smaller explicit counterexamples obtained

title: Exponential quantum space advantage in random data streams
comments: 27+3 pages. v2: fixed minor typos and added concurrent work statement
summary:
We show two unconditional quantum space advantages in the random-order streaming model. First, we show the Yamakawa-Zhandry Code Intersection problem admits exponential quantum advantage in the streaming model when its inputs are streamed in random order. This means quantum computers exhibit exponential space advantage even when simply receiving $(x,f(x))$ pairs for a uniformly random function $f$ in a uniformly random order. Notably, our classical space lower bound does not follow from a communication lower bound. Instead, we utilize density-restoring partitions from communication complexity directly with potential-function analysis in the style used to prove memory-sample tradeoffs for learning. The resulting argument is distinct from both lines of work.
  Second, we use our framework to show quantum space advantage for the Optimal Polynomial Intersection (OPI) problem in certain regimes via a streaming version of the Decoded Quantum Interferometry algorithm. In particular, we show that for degree $d$ and $n$ evaluation points, attaining $1/2 + Ω(\sqrt{d/n})$ fraction of satisfied OPI constraints via streaming requires $Ω(n)$ classical bits of memory but only $O(d\log n)$ qubits. This yields provable quantum advantage in a "low-rate" regime when the number of evaluation points is much larger than the degree, with a space advantage that can be as large as exponential in certain parameter settings.
comment: 27+3 pages. v2: fixed minor typos and added concurrent work statement

title: Fast mixing of the SYK model at high temperatures
comments: 34 pages; v2 improves exposition and updates references
summary: The Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev (SYK) model is a strongly interacting fermionic system. Its dynamics are difficult to analyze with Lieb-Robinson bounds and cluster expansions due to its all-to-all disordered interactions. We prove that, with high probability over the disorder, the SYK model admits a quantum Gibbs sampler with a system-size-independent spectral gap at sufficiently high constant temperatures. This yields polynomial-time preparation of SYK Gibbs states on a quantum computer. While prior non-rigorous computations that suggested SYK thermalization were limited to studying local correlators, we emphasize that our result holds up to arbitrary inverse polynomial trace distance. Our proof introduces the pseudo-Lindbladian approach to fermions then applies two key new ideas: a Bochner inequality for quantum dynamics, and an especially simple SYK analysis based on a comparison to classical dynamics.
comment: 34 pages; v2 improves exposition and updates references

title: Model-Based Koopman-Galerkin Lifting for Guaranteed H-Infinity Output Feedback Control of Nonlinear Systems
summary: In this paper, we present a model-based Koopman-Galerkin framework for output-feedback control of nonlinear systems with known dynamics. With a suitable actuator augmentation, the finite-dimensional realization preserves the actuator dynamics and the constant input matrix. The approach is based on an exact decomposition of the lifted dynamics into an LTI system and a finite-order closure residual. It also applies to non-control-affine systems and allows dictionaries that do not span an invariant subspace. Regional bounds are derived for the closure residual, actuator-realization defect, and output-reconstruction error. We use these bounds to formulate a standard $\mathcal{H}_\infty$ output-feedback problem. The controller is linear and dynamic and is implemented using only the measured tracking error. Neither full-state measurements nor a separate state observer are required. Lifting is performed offline. With the state coordinates retained in the dictionary, we obtain explicit transient bounds on the original state and tracking error. A sufficient condition for regional containment is also given. Under this condition, the nonlinear closed loop is forward complete, and the state and tracking error are uniformly ultimately bounded. The cart-pendulum example illustrates the nonlinear closed-loop guarantees. The proposed output feedback gives lower RMSE and peak tracking error on average than Jacobian-based $\mathcal{H}_\infty$ feedback, full-state backstepping, and Koopman-based hybrid MPC.

title: Improved Local Leakage Resilience of Shamir Secret Sharing and Worst-Case Optimal Polynomial Intersection
comments: 82 pages, 3 figures; v2 adds near-optimal OPI discrepancy for random Reed-Solomon codes
summary:
We study two problems: Local Leakage Resilience (LLR) for Shamir secret sharing, and worst-case Optimal Polynomial Intersection (OPI), over a prime field $\mathbb{F}_p$. For a polynomial $Q(X)$ of degree less than $k$, LLR for Shamir secret sharing asks what a few leaked bits from each of the $n$ shares $Q(α_1), \ldots, Q(α_n)$ reveal about $Q(0)$. Given (worst-case) input lists $S_1, \ldots, S_n \subset \mathbb{F}_p$, OPI seeks a polynomial $Q(X)$ so that $Q(α_i) \in S_i$ for as many $i$ as possible. Leveraging recent connections between these two problems due to (Sun, Wootters 2026), we improve the state-of-the-art for both problems.
  For LLR, we show that there is some constant $δ> 0$ so that Shamir secret-sharing is one-bit LLR (only a negligible amount about $Q(0)$ is learned) whenever $R := k/n \geq 1/2 - δ$. This is the first result to break the so-called ``one-half barrier'' for LLR, and improves over the previous best known result, requiring $R \geq 0.668$ (Kasser, 2025).
  For OPI, we give a quantum algorithm that finds a polynomial $Q(X)$ that agrees with at least a $\mathsf{SCL}_ρ(R)-\varepsilon$ fraction of the lists, for every fixed $\varepsilon>0$, where $\mathsf{SCL}_ρ$ is the \emph{semicircle law} of (Jordan et al., 2025). This improves previous algorithmic (and existential) results of (Jo, 2026) and (Horinaga, Yamakawa, 2026). We also give further improved existential results for all OPI instances; and when the evaluation points $α_i$ are chosen at random, for every rate $R > 0$ we show that, with high probability, for worst-case $S_i$ there exists \emph{perfect} solution. Finally, we adapt the hardness result of (Yamakawa, Zhandry, 2024) to apply to OPI (rather than a folded version); this gives an unconditional separation between the quantum and classical hardness of OPI relative to a membership oracle.
comment: 82 pages, 3 figures; v2 adds near-optimal OPI discrepancy for random Reed-Solomon codes

title: Near Minimax Rates for Quantile Distributional Reinforcement Learning
summary: In this paper, we study quantile distributional policy evaluation, where the return distribution under a given policy is approximated by the quantile Bellman fixed point $\bmη_m$. We investigate the statistical accuracy of estimating $\bmη_m$ across quantile resolutions under Wasserstein distances. Assuming access to a generative model, we construct a quantile fixed point estimator $\bmη_m^{(n)}$ from an empirical Markov decision process of $n$ observations per state-action pair and establish non-asymptotic error bounds under Wasserstein distances. When reward densities are uniformly bounded away from zero, we obtain a root-$n$ high-probability bound simultaneously over all resolutions $m$ and all Wasserstein orders $1\le p\le\infty$. When reward densities vanish at the support endpoints, we show that continuity and endpoint monotonicity suffice to preserve the same resolution-independent rate for $1\le p\le2$. For $p>2$, we establish a root-$n$ bound with coefficient $m^{1/2-1/p}$, together with a slower, resolution-independent $n^{-1/p}$ bound for every finite $p>2$. We further obtain resolution-independent $W_\infty$ consistency governed by the continuity modulus of reward quantile functions. To investigate the sharpness of these bounds, we characterize the exact local asymptotic minimax risk at each fixed resolution as the expected Wasserstein-coordinate norm of the efficient Gaussian limit and prove that our estimator attains it. We then examine the resolution dependence of this optimal local risk. A regular one-state instance has resolution-independent local risk constants, whereas a single endpoint-vanishing two-state instance exhibits growth of order $m^{1/2-1/p}$, up to logarithmic factors along a resolution subsequence, for every $p>2$.

title: Fitting Conventional and Neural Exchange-Correlation Functionals to Accurate Densities without Self-Consistent Fields
summary: Exchange-correlation functionals are usually fitted with energy-only losses, so better energies often bring worse densities. We introduce a workflow that predicts in closed form, from one Fock build on inverse Kohn-Sham orbitals of any accurate density, a functional's self-consistent density, and fits it to that density with no self-consistent-field solution. Fitted convexly, a CF22D-form hybrid beats CF22D and MN15 on unseen energies, dipole moments, and unfitted densities (6.8- and 22-fold lower density error). A neural meta-GGA fitted to 6 energies and 11 densities beats SCAN in both.

title: Optimality of the $D_4$ lattice quantizer
comments: Simplified the proof of four-dimensional optimality, with explicit polynomial certificates now included in the paper. Main results unchanged
summary: We prove that the root lattice $D_4$ uniquely minimizes the normalized second moment among four-dimensional lattices, up to similarity. The minimum is $13/(120\sqrt{2})$. The proof reduces the problem to polynomial inequalities on three secondary cones. We derive the second-moment formulas geometrically and give explicit polynomial certificates that can be checked by coefficient comparison. We also derive a lower bound for lattice quantizers in every dimension at least two from the number of Voronoi facets, using a comparison with circular cones and concavity in the solid angle. This bound strictly improves the sphere bound and recovers the hexagonal value in dimension two.
comment: Simplified the proof of four-dimensional optimality, with explicit polynomial certificates now included in the paper. Main results unchanged

title: Cyclotomic polynomials with trinomial irreducible factors over finite fields
summary: We classify the pairs $(q,n)$, where $q$ is a prime power, $n>1$, and $\gcd(n,q)=1$, for which every irreducible factor of $Φ_n(x)$ over $\F_q$ has exactly three nonzero terms. The positive support exponents of these factors have a common greatest common divisor, which gives a unique reduction by a power substitution. The reduced degree is two in odd characteristic and belongs to $\{2,3,4\}$ in characteristic two; the cubic and quartic cases arise by scalar substitution from the layers of orders $7$ and $15$. This yields necessary and sufficient arithmetic conditions on $(q,n)$ and explicit factorizations. Among the classified families, precisely those arising from quartic bases have a divisor layer containing an irreducible factor with more than three terms.

title: Seeing Why: Exact Evidence Maps for Quantum and Optical Image Classifiers
comments: 30 pages, 13 figures, 14 tables. Code, trained models and the IBM job records: https://github.com/stein-research/seeing-why (archived: doi:10.5281/zenodo.23906357). v2: abstract and introduction clarified (known identity vs. new measurement; Caltech-10 results marked exploratory), corresponding author, authors' ORCIDs, Zenodo DOI, clearer Figs. 9 and 12; results unchanged
summary: When an image classifier decides, we can usually only estimate why. For quantum and all-optical classifiers that act linearly on amplitude-encoded pictures up to the measurement, with no trained classical network before or after them, each class's Born probability above its no-information share, $P_g - b_g$, splits exactly into contributions of the encoded amplitudes, shown as Born evidence maps (BEM) over the picture. The split itself follows from known results on quadratic forms: with the transmitted light held fixed, it is what Integrated Gradients from a zero baseline and the Shapley value give. What we add is a way to measure it on the hardware that classifies, from class probabilities on a quantum chip or from camera frames on a lens bench, with no gradient circuit and no light sent backwards; a $g\times g$ map takes $1 + 2g^2$ runs. Deleting the 5% of pixels with the highest evidence drops accuracy from 73% to 9%, as occlusion does with 1,024 extra runs per picture, whereas gradient saliency removes much less. The classifiers share one architecture, a Fourier-plane mask followed by a brickwall circuit on qubits or by phase plates on a lens bench, read by a fixed Born headroom readout with no trained parameter; centring each picture on its own mean lets dark features count as much as bright ones. In simulation, four phase plates at a single wavelength reach 72.3% on Caltech-10 colour photographs. On IBM's ibm_kingston, with the mask applied before approximate loading, 300 test pictures were classified at 37.7% against 10% by chance (56.3% in exact simulation), and $2\times2$ maps of ten correctly classified pictures, one per class chosen by a stated rule, measured on the chip, agreed with the exact ones ($r = 0.77$). The maps also revealed a shortcut in the data; as the trim that removed it was chosen on test pictures, the Caltech-10 results are exploratory.

title: A Neuroprosthetic SoC Featuring Rapid Local Sensory Feedback with On-Chip Unsupervised Multi-Class Spike Sorting
comments: 4 pages, 9 figures, 3 tables. Author's accepted manuscript. Accepted for publication in IEEE Solid-State Circuits Letters
summary: This letter presents a 65 nm neuroprosthetic system-on-chip (SoC) featuring a rapid feedback pathway from motor recording to sensory stimulation. To enable low-latency sensory mapping modulated by individual-neuron firing rates, the SoC integrates a mixed-signal unsupervised spike-sorting module with stimulation-artifact rejection, a programmable sliding-window firing-rate calculator, and a closed-loop controller for adapting stimulation parameters. The spike-sorting module combines event-driven analog feature extraction with Manhattan-distance-based digital clustering while consuming 1.6 $μ$W/channel. On the Quiroga Difficult-1 benchmark, it achieves 94.58% three-class accuracy, with only a 0.4% reduction when stimulation artifacts are introduced at 20% of the spike count. The closed-loop controller supports polynomial and logarithmic mapping functions and incorporates Mitchell's approximation for power saving. The SoC is fully characterized on the bench and in vivo.
comment: 4 pages, 9 figures, 3 tables. Author's accepted manuscript. Accepted for publication in IEEE Solid-State Circuits Letters

title: Mission Capability-Aware UAV Swarm Coordination for Autonomous Disaster Response
summary: This paper proposes an artificial intelligence (AI) driven mission capability aware unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) swarm coordination framework for autonomous post disaster search and rescue. An integrated sensing and communication enabled master high altitude platform station senses the disaster environment, detects victims and hazards, and constructs adaptive rescue regions based on spatially varying mission demands. A mission capability requirement (MCR) quantifies regional capability demand, while a normalized mission capability score (MCS) characterizes the real time capability of individual UAVs. A capability-aware assignment mechanism matches UAV capabilities to regional requirements while minimizing deployment distance. An MCS based reallocation mechanism dynamically transfers UAVs from capability surplus to capability deficient regions while preserving donor sufficiency. A hierarchical deep reinforcement learning framework with proximal policy optimization performs high-level region selection, while MCR MCS matching enables feasible UAV level reallocation. Finally, joint trajectory optimization considers travel time, distance, propulsion energy, operational capability, obstacle avoidance, and inter UAV collision avoidance. Theoretical analysis and simulations demonstrate improved mission capability satisfaction, resource efficiency, and disaster response performance

title: Beyond TR 38.811 for 6G NTN Channel Models
summary: As the 3rd Generation Partnership Project (3GPP) expands 6G non-terrestrial network (NTN) to S, Ku, and Ka bands for integration with existing terrestrial cellular networks, the necessary satellite channel model for link and network performance evaluation remains tied to TR 38.811, last revised in 2020. We identify issues on multiple fronts: inappropriate parameter specifications based on very limited site-specific environments considered, omission of satellite-induced Doppler spread and directional antenna effects and lack of a transparent channel model generation procedure. To address these limitations, we re-derive the channel parameters using ray tracing (RT) over urban and rural environments based on ITU-R building statistics. Our results show that TR 38.811 substantially overestimates the K-factor at low elevations and predicts a decreasing trend with elevation, which is inconsistent with RT. The Ka-band clutter loss (CL) also exceeds the RT estimates by more than 15 dB in urban cases. It also underestimates rural delay spread (DS) at low elevations and predicts an elevation trend inconsistent with RT. We further quantify the previously neglected satellite-induced Doppler spread. Finally, we demonstrate that the conventional TR 38.811 channel generator significantly underestimates the K-factor in the presence of directional antenna (beamforming), while our modified generator substantially reduces this discrepancy.

title: GTAC: A Graph-Transformer Actor-Critic for Carrier-Aware MU-MIMO User Grouping
summary: Achieving higher spectral efficiency (SE) in 5G and future 6G networks requires efficient massive multi-user multiple-input multiple-output (MU-MIMO) grouping under coupled physical-layer constraints and strict scheduling deadlines. Motivated by industry efforts in AI-native RAN, we propose Graph-Transformer Actor-Critic (GTAC), a deep reinforcement learning (DRL) architecture for carrier-aware MU-MIMO user grouping. The objective is to maximize the long-term proportional-fair (PF) utility of the cell subject to constraints from the practical stack protocol. GTAC comprises a shared actor--critic encoder with spatial-edge-biased attention mechanism, a pointer decoder actor that generates grouping decisions, and a multi-stage transformer critic that estimates the carrier-wide state-value during training. Training begins by cloning a teacher policy that cannot meet real-time deployment deadlines, followed by critic warmup and two-stage reinforcement learning using proximal policy optimization (PPO), first on a narrow, power-matched carrier and then on the full carrier with a Kullback--Leibler (KL) policy anchor. After two-stage PPO, the best GTAC policy outperforms the non-real-time teacher by 11.6% in carrier SE, while exceeding its PF utility and preserving the cell-edge throughput. A CUDA implementation of GTAC achieves a 69.6 us inference latency on an RTX PRO 4500 GPU, below the targeted 100 us inference budget in practical systems.

title: RFShape: An IQ-Pretrained Wireless Foundation Model for Heterogeneous IQ & CIR Representations
summary: In wireless systems, foundation models have been proposed as alternative artificial intelligence models to replace task-specific models with a shared pretrained model that can be reused across many downstream applications (source separation, interference detection, localization, etc.). These wireless foundation models promise to reuse learned representations across diverse tasks, but choosing a foundation model also means choosing its input representation. For example, a model pretrained on spectrograms expects spectrograms, while one pretrained on in-phase/quadrature (IQ) samples expects IQ, limiting which pretrained model can be used for a given downstream problem. To remedy this, we present RFShape, a 7.4 M-parameter foundation model that breaks this coupling by adapting how a signal is presented to a shared pretrained encoder. RFShape is pretrained solely on synthetic IQ waveforms, without real captures, labels, or channel impulse responses (CIRs), and uses deterministic representation operators to support heterogeneous downstream inputs. Across ten tasks and nine datasets unseen during pretraining, the same encoder supports classification, ranging-error regression, and two-dimensional positioning. Representation selection alone increases 23-class radar recognition from 23.0% to 69.5% and short-range technology recognition from 70.8% to 97.1%. RFShape also outperforms CIR-pretrained ultra-wideband baselines by up to 12.7 percentage points for (N)LOS classification despite never observing CIRs during pretraining. These results show that foundation-model reuse need not be limited by the representation or modality seen during pretraining, and adapting how a signal is presented can extend a single pretrained encoder across heterogeneous wireless tasks.

title: Positioning and Radiation Efficiency Degrees of Freedom in Cascaded Pinching-Antenna Arrays
comments: 13 pages, 4 figures, 5 tables. Submitted to the IEEE Journal on Selected Areas in Communications
summary: In a pinching-antenna system (PASS), a single source feeds multiple pinches, resulting in a cascade that couples their radiated powers. A shared radiated-power limit, such as the interference power constraint in an underlay cognitive radio network, couples them again. We study such a network where PASS serves the secondary users. First, we formulate the joint optimization problem of the two degrees of freedom (DoF), pinch positions and radiation efficiencies, and characterize the single-link optimum analytically. Then, rather than proposing one method, we present the results for a grid of schemes whose two axes are the two DoF. Under an order-free attribution, positioning is worth 1.34 times radiation efficiency, and the two are near-perfect substitutes. We also show that substitutability is due to the constraint and not the cascade, since relaxing the constraint by 20 dB removes 97% of their interaction. At the joint reference, not knowing the primary receiver (PR) location costs 6.23 bit/s/Hz, more than twice the 2.87 that optimizing both DoF is worth. Instantaneous fading information adds a further 0.29 bit/s/Hz. Allocating efficiencies at equally spaced positions reaches 98% of the joint reference at about three orders of magnitude less computation.
comment: 13 pages, 4 figures, 5 tables. Submitted to the IEEE Journal on Selected Areas in Communications

title: Simulation-Driven Approach for Occlusion-Based Non-Line-Of-Sight Detection Using a Low-Cost Flash LiDAR
summary: Non-line-of-sight (NLOS) imaging aims to sense objects outside the direct line of sight. While most previous work focuses on the canonical around-the-corner configuration, this work considers a more challenging occlusion-based NLOS setting in which targets are hidden by scene geometry. To avoid the challenge of collecting large real-world datasets, we have developed a photon-based Monte Carlo simulator to generate diverse synthetic training data and validate against experimental data. We trained an AI model to identify multi-bounce photon patterns associated with hidden targets. The model achieves an Average Precision (AP) of 0.91 on synthetic test data and, when transferred directly to 180 real measurements acquired with a TMF8829 SPAD flash LiDAR, achieves 86.67% accuracy and an AP of 0.95. These results show that simulated transient data can support hidden-target detection with a low-cost commercial sensor and provide an initial step toward more general occlusion-based NLOS sensing and, ultimately, hidden-scene reconstruction.

title: Reconfigurable Antenna-Enhanced ISAC: A Unified Perspective on Electromagnetic Adaptation
summary: Integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) enables sensing and communication (S&C) functions to share time, frequency, and hardware resources, offering an efficient paradigm for next-generation wireless systems. However, conventional fixed-configuration antenna (FCA) architectures provide limited flexibility in adapting the physical electromagnetic (EM) response of the end-to-end wireless link. This article develops a unified EM-adaptation perspective on reconfigurable antenna (RA)-enhanced ISAC systems. We distinguish transceiver-side (TSc-side) and environment-side (Env-side) RA deployments and identify five fundamental EM reconfiguration dimensions: position, orientation, radiation pattern, polarization, and frequency response. Building on this framework, we examine how these dimensions customize communication channels, actively control target information mapping for sensing, and reshape the interplay between S&C, particularly by improving compatibility between S&C requirements under shared resources. Two case studies illustrate how TSc-side and Env-side EM reconfiguration can improve spatial selectivity and the achievable S&C performance tradeoff. Finally, we discuss several promising directions for advancing RA-enhanced ISAC systems, including fundamental performance limits, low-overhead black-box optimization, and artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled semantic ISAC.

title: ELiCv2: Learned LiDAR Geometry Compression under Real-Time Embedded Constraints
summary: Improving learned LiDAR compression increasingly relies on heavier inference, making it harder to meet the constraints of real-time embedded systems. We present ELiCv2, which removes two sources of redundant computation in progressive coding. Its discrete entropy interface selects a precomputed integer CDF instead of materializing one from a per-voxel distribution, while its occupancy-driven kernel-map builder derives finer-level sparse-convolution kernel-maps directly from the decoded hierarchy, eliminating coordinate-based neighbor search. ELiCv2 reinvests the recovered computation budget in lightweight ego-motion-aware temporal conditioning that gathers local occupancy context from the aligned previous reconstruction. On four LiDAR datasets and an NVIDIA Jetson Thor, ELiCv2 achieves a mean BD-rate reduction of 30.97% over G-PCC with channel width C=32 while sustaining the 20Hz nuScenes capture rate. Increasing the channel width to C=64 improves the mean reduction to 35.22%.

title: Toward Generalized LEO Channel Prediction: A Rapid Adaptation Time-Frequency Mamba Framework
comments: 6 pages, 7 figures, IEEE Global Communications Conference (GLOBECOM) 2026
summary: Accurate channel state information (CSI) prediction is pivotal for enhancing system capacity in low Earth orbit (LEO) satellite-terrestrial communications within the sixth-generation vision of global ubiquitous connectivity. However, the extreme mobility of LEO satellites, coupled with significant propagation delays, induces severe channel aging. Existing deep learning (DL) methods often struggle with non-stationary dynamics or generalize poorly across diverse global geographies. To address these challenges, we design the Evo-TFMamba, which is an evolutionary framework integrating time-frequency selective Mamba blocks with meta-learning for generalized CSI prediction. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed Evo-TFMamba performs adaptive prediction according to the geographic coverage of LEO satellites. Meanwhile, it significantly enhances the model's generalization ability, particularly when faced with unseen channel environments in LEO satellite communication.
comment: 6 pages, 7 figures, IEEE Global Communications Conference (GLOBECOM) 2026

title: Attendance-guided speaker enrollment across meetings
summary: Speaker-aware applications rely on enrolled voice profiles, yet collecting enrollment speech from every participant is impractical. Meeting archives provide an alternative source of enrollment speech, comprising recordings of recurring participants paired with expected attendance lists. We investigate whether expected attendance lists can be cross-referenced with diarized anonymous speaker clusters to identify reliable enrollment speech for recurring participants. The resulting task, multi-participant automatic enrollment, must accommodate two types of attendance noise: a listed participant may not speak, and a speaker may be unlisted. To this end, we introduce a benchmark for the task: a synthetic corpus calibrated to an in-house meeting corpus, paired with a contamination-sensitive evaluation protocol. The reference method we introduce scores cross-session cluster chains against expected-attendance patterns and abstains when the evidence is insufficient. We quantify the reference method's benchmark performance as a trade-off between enrollment success and contamination. Applying synthetic-development thresholds unchanged to real meetings exposes a synthetic-to-real gap that remains an open challenge. We will release the benchmark generator and evaluation code.

title: Movable Antenna Aided Robust Wireless Transmission: From Model-Based Optimization to Scalable Reinforcement Learning
comments: This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication. Copyright may be transferred without notice, after which this version may no longer be accessible
summary: This paper investigates robust joint antenna positioning and precoding for multiuser movable antenna (MA) systems under imperfect channel state information (CSI). First, we identify the mismatch between the spatial statistics of densely sampled MA channels and the discrete Fourier transform (DFT) basis used for conventional robust precoding. To address this, we develop a novel discrete prolate spheroidal sequence (DPSS)-based a posteriori channel model. By exploiting the spatial covariance structure of MA channels, this model is better suited to modeling MA channel uncertainty. Building on this model, we develop an efficient iterative algorithm for robust joint antenna positioning and precoding to maximize the expected sum rate. By transforming the coupled optimization of antenna positioning and precoding at each iteration into direct comparisons of closed-form scores, we design a low-complexity position replacement scheme that effectively reuses matrix computations across candidate sets. To further improve efficiency and scalability, we exploit the inherent tensor equivariance (TE) of the problem to develop a reinforcement learning framework. To explicitly account for channel uncertainty, we develop novel pairwise user-interaction and CSI-conditioned equivariant attention mechanisms to encode channel statistics and adaptively fuse them with the available CSI. We further introduce distance-biased spatial attention to incorporate the geometry of candidate positions into attention weighting, thereby enhancing spatial feature learning. Simulation results show that the proposed methods improve sum-rate performance while reducing online runtime under imperfect CSI. These methods also achieve near-optimal performance under perfect CSI, closely matching the exhaustive-search method. Moreover, the learning framework generalizes across different numbers of users and MAs without retraining.
